article.headline: The AI Money Loop That Never Quite Closes
article.lede: Sam Altman's OpenAI raised $122 billion in March 2026--a record by any measure. Much of that capital flows, almost immediately, back to the same handful of companies whose shares soared on the news.
article.body:
In March 2026, OpenAI closed what its press release called the largest private funding round in history: $122 billion at a post-money valuation of $852 billion. Among the headline investors were Amazon ($50 billion), NVIDIA ($30 billion), and SoftBank ($30 billion). The company's CFO went on television to celebrate. A week later, the Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI had quietly missed its internal revenue and user-growth targets, and that the same CFO was privately urging a delay to its planned IPO. The juxtaposition was clarifying.

The concern @DratchCap gestures at--with the knowing restraint of a chart 'presented without comment'--is what critics have taken to calling the **circular financing flywheel**: a self-referential loop in which OpenAI raises equity, deploys that equity to buy compute from NVIDIA, Oracle, and CoreWeave, and those same vendors announce enormous new chip orders or infrastructure buildouts that justify their own elevated valuations. NVIDIA, having received billions in chip revenue, then turns around and invests $30 billion back into OpenAI. The wheel keeps spinning; whether it is generating genuine momentum or merely the appearance of it is the question the chart invites.

The mechanics are not subtle. OpenAI signed a *letter of intent* with NVIDIA in September 2025 for up to $100 billion in chip and system purchases--a deal that, as late as December 2025, NVIDIA's own CFO admitted was not yet definitive. A separate $300 billion multi-year cloud-and-compute agreement with Oracle underpins the Stargate consortium, a joint venture announced at the White House alongside SoftBank and structured to spend up to $500 billion on U.S. AI infrastructure by 2029. Oracle, in turn, has committed to buying enormous quantities of NVIDIA hardware to fill those data centers. CoreWeave, the GPU-rental company that holds roughly $22 billion in OpenAI compute contracts, has meanwhile borrowed $8.5 billion against its GPU clusters and its customer backlog--with NVIDIA holding an equity stake and having committed to purchase $6.3 billion in CoreWeave's own cloud services. Each party is simultaneously a customer, a creditor, and a shareholder of the others.

None of this is, by itself, fraudulent. Economist Noah Smith has argued the arrangement more resembles legitimate vendor financing--analogous to General Motors funding car loans to move inventory--than the 'round-tripping' schemes that inflated revenues in the dot-com era. The underlying hardware is real, the data centers are being built, and the counterparties are public companies subject to audit. The more sober concern is about *incentive distortion* and *demand risk*: when the same capital recirculates through affiliated balance sheets, it can mask whether end-user demand is actually materializing fast enough to justify the infrastructure being financed. OpenAI says it is generating $2 billion in monthly revenue and $13.1 billion annually. Its CFO's reported private alarm--she warned colleagues that if growth did not accelerate, the company might struggle to fund its $600 billion-plus in outstanding infrastructure commitments--suggests the gap between contracted spend and organic revenue is uncomfortably wide.

The market, for its part, has begun to notice the dependency. When OpenAI's revenue miss leaked in late April 2026, shares of Oracle fell roughly 5 percent and CoreWeave fell a similar amount in a single session. NVIDIA dipped 1 percent. The stocks that had been buoyed by OpenAI's spending plans proved exposed to OpenAI's growth shortfall--precisely what you would expect if the revenues flowing through these deals are not yet self-sustaining. Whether the flywheel is building genuine escape velocity or simply buying time for the underlying AI economics to catch up remains, for now, an open question that the chart declines to answer.

concepts.definition: A pattern in which a central company (here, OpenAI) raises capital, spends it on goods and services from affiliated vendors, and those vendors then reinvest proceeds back into the original company--creating the appearance of robust commercial activity across the ecosystem without necessarily reflecting independent end-user demand. Critics compare it to 'round-tripping,' though defenders argue legitimate vendor financing looks structurally similar.

A joint venture announced in January 2025 by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, and MGX to build AI data center infrastructure across the United States, targeting up to $500 billion in investment by 2029. President Trump announced it at a White House press conference. Critics note the consortium's headline figures include planned spending, not committed capital.

A non-binding preliminary agreement outlining the terms two parties intend to formalize in a contract. In dealmaking, LOIs can be announced publicly and move markets even though they carry no legal obligation to complete. The NVIDIA-OpenAI $100 billion compute partnership was disclosed as an LOI and remained unsigned months later.

A company that rents access to graphics processing units--the specialized chips required to train and run large AI models--rather than selling them outright. CoreWeave is the largest independent GPU cloud provider; it finances its hardware purchases with debt secured against long-term customer contracts, making it structurally exposed to the creditworthiness of a small number of anchor clients.

An arrangement in which a supplier extends credit or equity investment to help a customer purchase its own products or services. Common in capital-intensive industries (aircraft, automobiles), it can be legitimate market-building or a warning sign that organic demand is insufficient to sustain the supplier's revenue at current levels.

article.fact_check: The NVIDIA-OpenAI $100 billion deal was disclosed as a letter of intent in September 2025; NVIDIA's CFO publicly noted in December 2025 that no definitive agreement had been signed. The $300 billion Oracle-OpenAI figure circulates widely in press coverage but no binding SEC-grade disclosure has been published--treat it as a reported framework, not a signed contract. OpenAI's $122 billion round and $852 billion valuation are confirmed by multiple sources as of March 31, 2026. The CFO tension over IPO timing and revenue targets was reported by the Wall Street Journal (April 28, 2026); OpenAI and CFO Sarah Friar called the report 'ridiculous' in a joint statement with Sam Altman.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_orcl.name: Oracle Corporation
ticker_orcl.blurb: Oracle is an enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company founded by Larry Ellison in 1977 and headquartered in Austin, Texas. Its core businesses are database software (Oracle Database remains the dominant enterprise RDBMS by revenue), cloud applications (ERP, HCM, and CX via Oracle Fusion and NetSuite), and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), its IaaS platform. OCI entered the AI infrastructure race later than AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud but has emerged as a preferred hyperscale partner for OpenAI and other large AI workloads, partly due to competitive GPU pricing and multi-region data-centre commitments. Oracle is an equity participant in the Stargate joint venture alongside OpenAI and SoftBank.
ticker_orcl.recent: Oracle's fiscal Q3 2026 (ending February 2026) was described by management as the strongest quarter in more than 15 years: total revenue rose 22% year-on-year to $17.2 billion, cloud revenue jumped 44% to $8.9 billion, and GPU-related cloud revenue grew 177% year-on-year in the prior quarter. The company reported a $523 billion remaining performance-obligation backlog — driven by AI mega-deals with OpenAI and Meta — and committed approximately $50 billion in capital expenditure for fiscal 2026. BNP Paribas analysts estimated that Oracle's 4.5 gigawatt Stargate capacity commitment could eventually generate $30–60 billion in annual revenue.

ticker_crwv.name: CoreWeave, Inc.
ticker_crwv.blurb: CoreWeave is a neocloud — a GPU-specialist cloud provider that rents NVIDIA accelerator capacity to AI developers, research labs, and enterprises rather than offering the broad service catalogue of a hyperscaler. Founded in 2017 as a cryptocurrency mining operation and pivoted to GPU cloud in 2019, it operates more than 40 data centres with roughly 250,000 NVIDIA GPUs. Its commercial model is long-term capacity contracts — often three to seven years — which produce a large, predictable backlog but require heavy upfront debt-financed capital expenditure. CoreWeave went public on NASDAQ on 28 March 2025 at $40 per share, valuing the company at approximately $23 billion fully diluted. NVIDIA invested $2 billion in CoreWeave at $87.20 per share in January 2026, cementing the symbiotic relationship between the two companies.
ticker_crwv.recent: CoreWeave reported $5.1 billion in revenue for full-year 2025, up 170% year-on-year, with quarterly revenue reaching $1.57 billion in Q4. Microsoft accounted for approximately 67% of FY2025 revenue. OpenAI has contracted up to $22.4 billion in cumulative commitments, and Meta signed a $14.2 billion agreement through December 2031. Total remaining performance obligations represent roughly 13 years of revenue at current run rates. In April 2026, CoreWeave priced an upsized $3.5 billion convertible senior notes offering and announced a multi-year GPU capacity agreement with Anthropic.
